crime: Every evening the linen-keeper carried the day's dried wash to the shower room in one chin-high stack — up the step-stool, onto the top shelf of the tall cupboard. One trip, never two. Most evenings the linen-keeper said it where the girls could hear: a second trip means the first one failed.
At supper the witch's stacked dishes slipped and broke. The linen-keeper knelt, gathered the pieces, and set them back in her hands — "again" — and the others laughed.

Years before, her hands had gone wrong at the one audition that decided her life: a piece she had played without error many times came apart that morning, the place went to another girl, and no second audition was offered.

The next evening, after the linen-keeper's shelving, the witch spoke the binding over her in passing — the nightly carry was the bound act. Once the showers were empty she pulled everything from the cupboard, tipped it back against the wall, and ground its front feet down — enough that a loaded top shelf would carry the cupboard forward past balance. She set it upright, returned the wash to the lower shelves, and left the top shelf empty.

The next night the linen-keeper loaded the top shelf, and the front feet let the top-heavy cupboard pitch forward. Any other girl would have dropped the wash and stepped off the stool, but both are a breaking-off partway, and the binding allowed none. The linen-keeper did neither, and the cupboard came down.

At the night lock the linen-keeper's cell was empty. The girls who went looking found the linen-keeper in the shower room, crushed beneath the toppled cupboard, the wash still on its shelves, the step-stool in place.
The cupboard's front feet were ground to raw, pale wood. On the floor beneath, wood dust a sweep had missed.
The last girl out of the showers the night before had seen her at the cupboard after the linen-keeper had gone, with nothing of her own to dry and no wash to shelve.
fields.epitaph: Her life was one morning long, and she never gave anyone a second.
fields.epithet: She Who Handed Back the Day, Whole
execution: A single blade hung on a threaded rod above the execution stand. The rod crept downward.
At her hand was a single lever she could throw once. Thrown at the one right instant, it would stop the blade for good; at any other instant, or not at all, the rod would run its full descent.
Nothing marked the right instant. There was nothing to read and nothing to count.
She threw. The rod did not stop. It ran to its end, and the blade came down.

magic.name: All or Nothing
magic.text: She names aloud one act of one person in her presence and binds it; the next time that person does the act, it goes flawlessly or fails outright — no partial outcome, no stopping partway, no second attempt.
